title: Politics in India: India's External Relations

topics.title: India's foreign policy: context, Article 51 and Nehru's goals

learn.hook: India became free just as the Cold War split the world into two armed camps. A poor, newly independent country had to find its own way between them.
points: India became independent in a world shaped by the Cold War rivalry between the USA-led and USSR-led blocs. Newly independent India wanted to protect its freedom while building its economy.

Article 51 of the Constitution, a Directive Principle of State Policy, asks the state to promote international peace and security, maintain just and honourable relations between nations, foster respect for international law and treaty obligations, and encourage settlement of international disputes by arbitration.
Jawaharlal Nehru was both Prime Minister and Foreign Minister from 1946 to 1964, and he played a central role in shaping India's foreign policy.
Nehru's three major objectives: to preserve the hard-earned sovereignty of the country, to protect its territorial integrity, and to promote rapid economic development.

example.q: Which part of the Constitution guides India's foreign policy towards peace, and what does it say?
steps: It is Article 51, in the Directive Principles of State Policy.
It asks the state to promote international peace and security and just relations between nations.
It also asks for respect for international law and settlement of disputes by arbitration.
example.answer: Article 51: promote peace and security, just relations, respect for international law, settlement by arbitration

learn.reallife: When Indian diplomats call for dialogue and peaceful settlement at the UN, they are echoing the spirit of Article 51.

learn.hook: Choosing not to join either superpower's camp did not mean sitting on the fence. Non-alignment let India decide each issue on its merits.
points: Non-alignment meant keeping away from the military alliances of both the US-led and the Soviet-led blocs, while staying free to take an independent position on each issue.
Non-alignment was not isolation or neutrality: India took active stands, for example on decolonisation and disarmament, and developed relations with both blocs.
India championed Afro-Asian unity. Nehru convened the Asian Relations Conference in New Delhi in March 1947, before independence.
The Afro-Asian conference at Bandung, Indonesia, in 1955 marked a high point of solidarity among newly independent countries and paved the way for the Non-Aligned Movement.
The first summit of the Non-Aligned Movement (NAM) was held in Belgrade in September 1961. Nehru was a co-founder, along with Josip Broz Tito of Yugoslavia and Gamal Abdel Nasser of Egypt.

example.q: Order: First NAM summit; Asian Relations Conference; Bandung Conference.
steps: March 1947: Asian Relations Conference, New Delhi.
1955: Bandung Conference, Indonesia.
1961: First NAM summit, Belgrade.

learn.reallife: India still describes its foreign policy as one of 'strategic autonomy', a modern descendant of non-alignment.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'If India didn't join either bloc, did it just stay quiet?'
teach.praise: Not quiet at all! Non-alignment kept India out of military blocs but active on issues, from the 1947 Asian Relations Conference to Bandung and NAM in Belgrade in 1961!
teach.nudge: Good. Where and when was the first NAM summit, and who were its founders?

learn.hook: In 1954 India and China agreed on five principles for living as good neighbours. Five years later, a young monk crossed the Himalayas into India, and the friendship began to strain.
points: Panchsheel, the five principles of peaceful coexistence, was signed by Nehru and Chinese Premier Zhou Enlai on 29 April 1954.

The five principles: mutual respect for each other's territorial integrity and sovereignty; mutual non-aggression; mutual non-interference in each other's internal affairs; equality and mutual benefit; and peaceful coexistence.
Tibet had historically been an area of friction. China took control of Tibet in 1950, and India did not openly oppose it.
In 1959 a rebellion broke out in Tibet. The Dalai Lama crossed into India and sought political asylum, which India granted. China strongly objected, and relations worsened.

example.q: List the five principles of Panchsheel.
steps: 1. Mutual respect for territorial integrity and sovereignty.
2. Mutual non-aggression.
3. Mutual non-interference in internal affairs.
4. Equality and mutual benefit.
5. Peaceful coexistence.
example.answer: Territorial integrity and sovereignty; non-aggression; non-interference; equality and mutual benefit; peaceful coexistence

learn.reallife: Dharamshala in Himachal Pradesh has hosted the Dalai Lama and a large Tibetan community since he sought asylum in India.

topics.title: The Chinese aggression of 1962 and after

learn.hook: In October 1962 Chinese troops attacked across the Himalayas. The short war shook India's confidence and changed its politics.
points: Border disputes, mainly over Aksai Chin in the Ladakh region and much of what was then NEFA (now Arunachal Pradesh), had grown after the 1950s.
In October 1962 China launched a swift and massive invasion on both disputed regions. India's forces were unprepared, and China declared a unilateral ceasefire after advancing.
The defeat hurt India's image and Nehru's standing. Defence Minister V.K. Krishna Menon had to leave the cabinet. The first no-confidence motion against Nehru's government was moved in the Lok Sabha.
The war also affected domestic politics: differences over China contributed to the split in the Communist Party of India in 1964.

Normalisation took time: full diplomatic relations were restored in 1976. Atal Bihari Vajpayee visited China as External Affairs Minister in 1979, and Rajiv Gandhi's 1988 visit started a new phase of ties.

example.q: List two domestic consequences of the 1962 war in India.
steps: Defence Minister V.K. Krishna Menon had to leave the cabinet.
The first no-confidence motion against the Nehru government was moved; the CPI later split partly over China.
example.answer: Krishna Menon's exit; first no-confidence motion against Nehru (and the CPI split)

learn.reallife: India later created strong mountain divisions and built roads and tunnels in Ladakh and Arunachal Pradesh, partly as a lesson from 1962.

topics.title: Wars and peace with Pakistan: 1947-48 to 1965

learn.hook: Within weeks of independence, India and Pakistan were at war over Kashmir. Yet in 1960 they signed a water treaty that survived the wars of 1965 and 1971.
points: Soon after independence, a conflict broke out over Kashmir in 1947-48, often described as a proxy war, when Pakistan backed armed raiders. It ended with a ceasefire, and the issue was taken to the UN.
Despite conflict, the two countries cooperated on some issues. The Indus Waters Treaty was signed in 1960 by Nehru and General Ayub Khan, with the World Bank's mediation.

In 1965 Pakistan launched armed attacks in the Rann of Kutch area of Gujarat in April, followed by a bigger offensive in Jammu and Kashmir in August-September. Prime Minister Lal Bahadur Shastri ordered Indian forces to respond, and they advanced close to Lahore.
The war ended with UN intervention. The Tashkent Agreement was signed in January 1966 by Shastri and General Ayub Khan, brokered by the Soviet Union.

example.q: Match each agreement to its mediator: Indus Waters Treaty; Tashkent Agreement.
steps: Indus Waters Treaty (1960): World Bank.
Tashkent Agreement (1966): Soviet Union.
example.answer: Indus - World Bank; Tashkent - Soviet Union

learn.reallife: Canals fed by the Indus system water fields across Punjab, Haryana and Rajasthan, which is why the 1960 treaty mattered so much to farmers.

topics.title: The Bangladesh War of 1971 and the Kargil conflict

learn.hook: In December 1971, within about two weeks, India's forces helped create a new nation. Nearly three decades later, Indian soldiers fought on icy peaks in Kargil.
points: In 1970 East Pakistan voted overwhelmingly for the Awami League, but the West Pakistan leadership refused to accept the result. The Pakistani army began a crackdown in 1971, and about 80 lakh refugees fled to India.
India faced a hostile combination of the USA, Pakistan and China. To counter this, India signed a 20-year Treaty of Peace and Friendship with the Soviet Union in August 1971.

Full-scale war broke out in December 1971. Indian forces, with the support of local people, advanced quickly; within about ten days they had surrounded Dhaka, and the Pakistani army surrendered. Bangladesh became independent.
The Shimla Agreement between Indira Gandhi and Zulfikar Ali Bhutto, signed in 1972, formalised the return of peace.
In 1999 Pakistani forces and militants occupied heights in the Kargil sector (including Mashkoh, Dras, Kaksar and Batalik). India responded strongly and recaptured the positions.

example.q: Why did India sign the Treaty of Peace and Friendship with the USSR in 1971?
steps: The USA and China were moving closer, with Pakistan's help.
India faced a possible hostile combination over the Bangladesh crisis.
A treaty with the USSR gave India diplomatic and possible military support.
example.answer: To counter the US-China-Pakistan combination during the Bangladesh crisis

learn.reallife: Kargil Vijay Diwas is observed every year on 26 July in memory of the soldiers who fought in 1999.

learn.hook: Nehru called for the world to give up nuclear weapons. Decades later India tested its own. The story of India's nuclear policy is about principle meeting security.
points: Nehru had great faith in science and technology for building modern India, and he opposed nuclear weapons, pleading for comprehensive nuclear disarmament. The atomic energy programme was led by Homi J. Bhabha.

India conducted its first nuclear explosion at Pokhran in May 1974, calling it a peaceful nuclear explosion. In May 1998 India carried out a series of nuclear tests, and Pakistan tested soon afterwards.

India refused to sign the NPT (1968) and the CTBT (Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty, 1996), calling them discriminatory because they allow existing nuclear powers to keep their weapons while denying others.

India's nuclear doctrine: no first use (India will not be the first to use nuclear weapons) and credible minimum nuclear deterrence. India remains committed to global, verifiable and non-discriminatory nuclear disarmament.
Exercise tip: order foreign policy events by date and explain NAM and its relevance.

example.q: Explain India's nuclear doctrine in two phrases.
steps: No first use: India will use nuclear weapons only in retaliation.
Credible minimum deterrence: enough capability to deter an attack, not an arms race.
example.answer: No first use; credible minimum deterrence

learn.reallife: India's civilian nuclear power plants, run by the Nuclear Power Corporation, and research at the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre in Mumbai grew from the programme Homi Bhabha began.
